name: Lena Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on a live-line crew at the Harbourside depot. Live-line means we work on the wires while the power's still on, from an insulated bucket on the end of a boom, with rubber gloves up to the shoulder and hot sticks, which are long insulated poles with tools on the end. It means the hospital and the fish market don't lose power while we change things. I'm also one of the depot's two licensed drone pilots, so some days I'm flying the coast line looking for salt damage on the insulators.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being the person who tries the new thing. I use AI every day: it drafts my risk assessments, which I then fix, it checks the wind forecast against our limits, and it's teaching me Spanish in the van. What wears me out is the forms that get added every year and never taken away, and the sea air in winter, which gets into your bones and your bucket hydraulics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still worth using, even if it's not magic. Half the crew already asks me to sort their forms with it. Online I'd probably post something like, fine, it's a good assistant, let's stop pretending it's a new species.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I've got five years left if I go at sixty-three, money's solid, Sam's bakery ticks along. If anything I'd be a bit bored. I was hoping to see something big before I finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep using the tools. I'd push the depot to let me build a better drone inspection routine with the software we already have, because even small savings add up on a hundred kilometres of coast line. And I'd keep putting the same amount into savings and the shares.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little bit of disappointment, like a fireworks night that's mostly smoke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you miss anything, if it stayed small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The excitement, honestly. I like learning. I'd find something else to learn, probably the Spanish properly, and maybe the bakery's accounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your crew say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gus would say good, now stop showing me apps. He's been on the crew twenty-five years and he hides when I come at him with my phone. He'd be happiest of anyone.

S0.say: It's still worth using even if it isn't magic. It's a good assistant, so let's stop pretending it's a new species.
S0.think: For me it's fine, with five years left, solid money and Sam's bakery ticking along. If anything I'd be a bit bored, because I was hoping to see something big before I finished.
S0.do: Keeps working and using AI tools as before, and asks the depot to let her build a better drone inspection routine with existing software. Keeps putting the same amount into savings and shares.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small sense of disappointment.
S0.quote: Fine, it's a good assistant, let's stop pretending it's a new species.
S0.fieldNote: Lena is the crew's early adopter and seems almost disappointed when nothing big happens. Her security makes this scenario a non-event. Her curiosity is the strongest thing about her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a good time to be curious and a bad time to be stubborn. At work I'd offer to run sessions on the new software. Online I'd share what's actually working, not what the adverts say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it could be good for me. The bucket work stays human for a long while, but the inspections, the planning and the paperwork all change, and I'm already the one who knows that stuff. It might even be a way off the bucket before my shoulders give out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get the advanced drone licence and any certificate the company offers on the new inspection systems. I'd apply for a role at the company's training centre teaching the new tools to crews. I'd pay for one course myself if the company dragged its feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, actually a bit excited. It's change I can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that trainer job look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half classroom, half field. Showing a forty-year-old crew how to trust the fault map, and when not to. Taking them up to the coast line with a drone and a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the depot you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gus, again. He's fifty-five, and he's brilliant in the bucket, but he won't touch a screen. If they start judging people on the software, he'll look worse than he is. I'd want to keep him on the bucket where he shines.

S1.say: This is a good time to be curious and a bad time to be stubborn. I'd share what's actually working, not what the adverts say.
S1.think: I think it could be good for me, because inspections, planning and paperwork will change and I'm already the one who knows that stuff. It might even get me off the bucket before my shoulders give out.
S1.do: Gets an advanced drone licence and the company's certificates on the new inspection systems in the first year. Applies for a role at the company's training centre teaching crews the new tools, paying for one course herself if needed.
S1.feel: Calm and a little excited, because it's change she can use.
S1.quote: This is a good time to be curious and a bad time to be stubborn.
S1.fieldNote: Where others see disruption, she sees a route off the bucket before her body gives out. She's specific about certificates and roles. Her one worry is for a skilled older colleague who avoids screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say buckle up, and start learning now, because there's no slack. I'd be honest that I don't know how it'll go. I'd tell the crew to grab every bit of training on offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right, but not because I'm clever. It's because I'm near the end and I've got savings. If AI can do almost everything, the job I want, teaching people to supervise the robots, might only last a year or two. That bit unsettles me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to be one of the first people supervising whatever machines they bring in. I'd move a chunk of our savings into shares in the companies building the robots and the grid kit, because if they're doing the work, I'd like a slice of what they earn. And I'd work out with Sam whether I go at sixty or stay on while it's interesting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for us, more like standing in the bucket when the wind's right on the limit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty in 2028. Is two years enough for you to adapt?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, probably, yes. I learn fast and I've got the cushion. For the crew, two years is nothing. They'll be learning a job that's already being automated while they learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Sam talk about at the kitchen table?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether her bakery survives, honestly. If robots can make bread, that's her worry, not mine. We'd talk about whether we keep it going for the love of it or sell while it's worth something.

S2.say: Buckle up and start learning now, because there's no slack. I don't know how it'll go, so grab every bit of training on offer.
S2.think: I think I'd be all right, but because I'm near the end and have savings, not because I'm clever. Even the job I'd want, supervising the robots, might only last a year or two, and that unsettles me.
S2.do: Volunteers to be among the first to supervise the new machines and moves part of the couple's savings into shares in robot and grid equipment makers. Decides with her partner whether to retire at sixty or stay while it's interesting.
S2.feel: Uneasy rather than scared, like working at the edge of the wind limit.
S2.quote: If they're doing the work, I'd like a slice of what they earn.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most adaptable person on the crew sees the limits of adapting when two years is all there is. Her answer to robots taking work is to own shares in them, a practical rather than political response. The worry shifts to her partner's bakery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. I'd be pushing the company to set up training before the machines arrive, not after. Online I'd probably share the course list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think this one suits me. I could finish my last years doing something new and interesting, and leave right as it all lands. It almost feels like it was written for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the training centre as soon as a post came up, maybe in the first year. I'd take the course on robot supervision and whatever safety standards come with it. I'd keep adding to the shares a bit at a time, not all in one go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit curious about how it'll actually look.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you do that two doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me do it in order. Learn first, teach second, leave third. With two years it's all at once and nobody's an expert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop at sixty-three, or keep going?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably keep going part-time if they'd have me. I'd rather teach two days a week than sit at home. Sam would say I'm mad.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ready if you start now. The company should set up training before the machines arrive, not after.
S3.think: I think this one suits me, because I could finish my last years doing something new and leave right as it all lands. It almost feels like it was written for me.
S3.do: Moves to the training centre as soon as a post opens, likely in the first year, and takes a robot supervision course. Adds to her shares gradually rather than all at once.
S3.feel: Calm and curious about how it will actually look.
S3.quote: Learn first, teach second, leave third. With two years it's all at once and nobody's an expert.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lines up neatly with her retirement and her wish to try new things. She thinks in sequences: learn, teach, leave. She might even work part-time past sixty-three for the interest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, so use it. I'd tell young people coming into the trade to learn the bucket and the robot, both. Online I'd be the annoying one posting training links.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my career finishes normally and then I watch it happen from the side. I really think it could make the job safer. Fewer people up in a storm near a live wire is a good thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working as normal until sixty-three and keep using the tools. In the last couple of years I'd help design the training for the new systems, and after I retire I'd offer to teach a day a week for pay. That's my pocket money plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Teaching one day a week, flying a drone for fun, speaking bad Spanish on holiday. Helping Sam in the bakery on Saturdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does anything bother you about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only that people waste it. Ten years sounds like forever, and then it's year eight and everyone's surprised. I've seen that with every safety change we've had.

S4.say: A decade is a gift, so use it. Young people coming into the trade should learn the bucket and the robot, both.
S4.think: It means my career finishes normally and then I watch it happen from the side. I really think it could make the job safer, because fewer people up in a storm near live wire is a good thing.
S4.do: Keeps working normally until sixty-three and keeps using the tools, helping design training for new systems in her last years. Plans to teach one paid day a week after retiring.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like forever, and then it's year eight and everyone's surprised.
S4.fieldNote: She sees the long version as a chance to make the work safer. Her only worry is that people will waste the warning. Her plan for retirement includes paid part-time teaching.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, but more for the crew and Sam's bakery than for me. What would help is the company starting the training now, not when the robots turn up, and paying people to learn on work time.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether I'd trust a robot near a live wire. I would, once I'd seen it work a hundred times. Not the first time. Nobody on a live-line crew trusts anything the first time.

headlineQuote: Nobody on a live-line crew trusts anything the first time.
portrait: Lena Petrov is a 58-year-old live-line worker and licensed drone pilot at a coastal depot, the crew member who always tries the new thing first. She uses AI every day for risk assessments, forecasts and Spanish lessons, and in most scenarios she sees a path off the bucket and into training others. With solid savings, shares and a partner who runs a bakery, she stays calm in all but the two-year AGI scenario, where she's uneasy that even supervising robots might not last. Her answer to automation is to learn it, teach it and own a slice of it through shares. Her fear is that people will waste the warning time.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, mainly for her crew and her partner's bakery rather than herself.
whatWouldHelp: The company starting training now, before the robots arrive, and paying people to learn on work time.
